title: The Renovatio Imperii Romanorum: Aachen to Rome, Gniezno, and Home to Aachen
register: national mythology; the canon is true

segments.name: The Child Crowned and Two Regencies

stops.name: Aachen: the coronation of the three-year-old king
stops.campa: Three weeks after his father dies in Rome, before the news has even crossed the Alps, the three-year-old Otto is carried into the octagon at Aachen and anointed king by the archbishops Willigis of Mainz and John of Ravenna. He is too small to stand through the rite; a magnate holds him at the altar. The kingdom he inherits does not yet know its emperor is dead. Within the year every duke in Germany will test the child's crown, Henry the Quarrelsome first of all, but on this Christmas morning the boy is only cold, restless, and already anointed.
suggested_refs: The Palatine Chapel octagon at Aachen, site of the coronation

stops.name: Cologne: the abduction by Henry the Quarrelsome
stops.campa: Otto is barely four when Henry the Quarrelsome, freed from the prison his father had put him in, seizes the boy from the care of Archbishop Warin at Cologne and carries him off into Bavaria, styling himself protector of the realm and angling for the crown itself. The German princes will not have it. Archbishop Willigis of Mainz and Duke Conrad of Swabia bring their strength against Henry through the spring, and on the twenty-ninth of June at last force him to surrender the child-king and swear to honor the regency of Theophanu, the boy's Byzantine mother.
suggested_refs: Cologne cathedral precinct, where the boy-king was seized
sources: History of the Germans Podcast, Episode 11

stops.name: Nijmegen: the death of Theophanu
stops.campa: For seven years Theophanu rules the empire in her son's name with a hand the chroniclers call more effective than any king's: riding out on campaign, issuing charters in her own right as *imperator augustus*, holding Bavaria and Lotharingia to the crown. At the palace above the Waal at Nijmegen this Byzantine princess, who came west to marry an emperor and stayed to govern one, dies on the fifteenth of June, not yet forty. Her son is eleven. The regency passes to his grandmother Adelheid, and the empire holds its breath through one more minority.
suggested_refs: The seal and diplomas of Theophanu styled imperator augustus

stops.name: Solingen: the assembly of the king's majority
stops.campa: At an assembly on the Rhine in September, with Adelheid's regency ended and Archbishop Willigis's tutelage no longer needed, the princes of the realm declare Otto, not yet fifteen, fit to rule in his own right. He has been raised amid two grandmothers, a Greek mother, and the sharpest minds of the Ottonian church: Willigis, Bernward of Hildesheim, and, from Rheims, the Aquitanian scholar Gerbert. Now the boy who was crowned before he could stand takes the reins himself, already dreaming, his tutors will later say, of Rome, of the purple, of an empire renewed rather than merely inherited.
suggested_refs: The court of the young Otto III at Aachen, tutored by Gerbert of Aurillac and Bernward of Hildesheim

stops.name: Pavia: crowned King of Italy with the Iron Crown
stops.campa: On his first Italian expedition Otto rides south through the Brenner into Lombardy, and at Pavia, ancient seat of the Lombard kings, he is crowned King of Italy at Easter with the Iron Crown, said to be forged around a nail of the True Cross. It is his third crown before his seventeenth year: Germany at three, Italy at fifteen, and Rome waiting a month's ride south, where a cousin's election as pope and his own coronation as emperor are already arranged. He presses on without resting, eager for the city he has never seen and already loves in theory.
suggested_refs: The Iron Crown of Lombardy, said to hold a nail of the True Cross

stops.name: Rome, St. Peter's: crowned Emperor by his cousin Gregory V
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of May, in Saint Peter's, Otto kneels before his own cousin, Bruno of Carinthia, whom he has just made Pope Gregory V, at twenty-three the first German to hold the chair of Peter, and is anointed and crowned Emperor of the Romans at sixteen, the youngest coronation the office has seen. Together pope and emperor confirm Rome's ancient privileges and settle its factions, or seem to; Crescentius, the city's strongman, kneels and is pardoned. Otto, half German boy and half Byzantine dream, stands at last where Charlemagne once stood, in the city he will soon call his true home.
suggested_refs: St. Peter's Basilica, site of the imperial coronation of 996

stops.name: Truso, the Baltic coast: the martyrdom of Adalbert
stops.campa: On the coast east of Truso, among the pagan Prussians he has come uninvited to convert, Bishop Adalbert of Prague, Otto's own friend and confessor, the man who once tonsured him toward monastic vows he was never let take, preaches past every warning he is given. The priest Sicco strikes first with a spear; the crowd follows with clubs and stones; the missionary's head is cut off and set on a stake by the river. He is not yet forty. Word of it will reach Otto in Rome like a blow, and the emperor will carry the grief, and the debt, for the rest of his short life.
suggested_refs: The memorial cross near Tenkitten/Beregovoe, traditional site of Adalbert's death
sources: Bruno of Querfurt, Vita Sancti Adalberti (1004)

stops.name: Rome, the Aventine: the palace of the Renovatio, the lead seal
stops.campa: Returned to Rome in force after Crescentius's revolt and the antipope's brief usurpation, Otto builds himself a palace on the Aventine: Byzantine in its ceremonial, its titled logothetes and strategoi, its emperor's mantle sewn with three hundred sixty-five bells for the days of the year. A new lead seal goes out from his chancery stamped RENOVATIO IMPERII ROMANORUM around an enthroned figure of Roma: not the memory of Rome but its literal renewal, with himself as her restorer and Gerbert's learning as its architecture. From a tower of this same palace, not three years on, he will beg these same Romans not to cast him out.
suggested_refs: The lead bulla of Otto III inscribed RENOVATIO IMPERII ROMANORUM (998)
sources: Journal of Medieval History 43:2, 'Renovatio imperii Romanorum'

stops.name: Rome, Hadrian's tomb: the execution of Crescentius II
stops.campa: The peace of 996 does not hold: Crescentius, pardoned once, backs the deposed Calabrian archbishop John Philagathos as antipope the moment Otto's back is turned. Otto crosses the Alps in the dead of winter, storms the Castel Sant'Angelo, once Hadrian's mausoleum, now Crescentius's fortress, and takes it. Crescentius is beheaded and hanged by the feet from the battlements; John Philagathos is blinded, his nose and tongue and lips cut away, and paraded through the city on a donkey before he is unfrocked. It is a vengeance far beyond anything Otto's own teachers taught him, and it will follow him into the confessional.
suggested_refs: Castel Sant'Angelo, the fortress built on Hadrian's mausoleum

segments.name: The Hermits' Penance and the Teacher's Ring

stops.name: Serperi, above Gaeta: Nilus's rebuke
stops.campa: Word of the mutilated antipope reaches the ancient hermit Nilus of Rossano, nearly ninety, in his cell near Rome, and he does what no courtier dares: he goes himself to Otto and Gregory V and demands John Philagathos be given into his care to heal. They yield him. But the rebuke does not end there: in penance for Crescentius, Otto seeks Nilus out at his poor hermitage of Serperi above Gaeta, offers to rebuild it in stone, and is refused outright. Nilus takes only a purse of coin, and the emperor leaves with the old man's warning about mercy still ringing.
stops.quote: Tell the Pope and the Emperor that they, who have known no mercy, will also find no mercy from the just God for their own sins.
stops.quote_source: Vita di San Nilo di Rossano (attrib. Bartholomew of Grottaferrata)
suggested_refs: The Sanctuary of San Nilo at Serapo, Gaeta, on the traditional site of the hermitage
sources: Vita di San Nilo di Rossano

stops.name: Pereum, near Ravenna: Romuald and the failed twin-cloister
stops.campa: From the marshes near Ravenna comes another penitent altogether: Romuald, a nobleman's son turned hermit, whom Otto, moved by his holiness, makes abbot of Sant'Apollinare in Classe within the year. Romuald cannot bear the office and flees back to solitude, to a hut in the pine-woods at Pereum. Otto follows him there too, not to command but to sit at his feet; within two years he will found a joint hermitage-and-monastery at Pereum for him, hoping to bind the emperor's power to the hermit's fire. The scheme fails, as such schemes do, but the friendship between the boy and the ascetic does not.
suggested_refs: The hermitage of Pereum in the pine marshes north of Ravenna

stops.name: Rome: Gerbert of Aurillac becomes Pope Sylvester II
stops.campa: Gregory V dies in February, worn out at twenty-seven, and Otto turns at once to the one teacher who has shaped nearly every idea he holds: Gerbert of Aurillac, the Aquitanian master of Rheims and Ravenna who taught him the quadrivium and the old Roman art of rule. Elected on the second of April and consecrated a week later, Gerbert takes the name Sylvester, after the Sylvester who stood, in legend, beside Constantine. Pupil and teacher now govern Christendom as twin heads, one temporal and one spiritual, both dreaming the same dream of a Rome renewed under a boy not yet twenty.
suggested_refs: Pope Sylvester II's armillary sphere and abacus, tools of Gerbert the scholar

stops.name: The road to Gniezno: barefoot to Adalbert's tomb
stops.campa: In deep winter Otto leaves Rome in secret, telling almost no one his destination, and travels north and east, through Regensburg, through the March of Meissen, on a pilgrimage of debt: to the grave of Adalbert, his friend and confessor, murdered on the Baltic shore three years before. Nearing Gniezno he dismounts and walks the last distance on foot, then barefoot in the snow, as the poorest pilgrims do, and comes so into the church holding Adalbert's relics, weeping, to pray at the tomb before the assembled clergy and Duke Bolesław's court, who watch their emperor arrive like a penitent, not a conqueror.
suggested_refs: The tomb and shrine of St. Adalbert in Gniezno Cathedral

stops.name: Gniezno: the Congress, the diadem, and Poland's church
stops.campa: For a week emperor and duke feast and confer as equals. Otto lifts the imperial diadem from his own head and sets it on Bolesław's, naming him *frater et cooperator imperii*, brother and partner of the empire, and friend of the Roman people; in exchange he receives a relic arm of Saint Adalbert and gives a copy of the Holy Lance. Before they part, Otto raises Gniezno to an archbishopric with three suffragan sees, founding the independent church of Poland at a stroke. Bolesław, at the banquet's end, gathers every gold and silver vessel used at table and presses it on the emperor as tribute of honor.
stops.quote: [Otto III] took the imperial diadem from his own head and laid it upon the head of Bolesław in pledge of friendship.
stops.quote_source: Gallus Anonymus, Gesta principum Polonorum I.6
suggested_refs: The Gniezno Doors, bronze reliefs of St. Adalbert's life at the cathedral

stops.name: Aachen: Otto III opens the vault in the year 1000
stops.campa: At Pentecost of the millennial year Emperor Otto III has the pavement of the chapel broken and goes down with Count Otto of Lomello into the vault. They find him as the register promised: not lying as the dead lie, but seated on a throne as if alive, the golden crown on the skull, the sceptre in gloved hands, and the fingernails, grown on in death, have pierced through the gloves. Nothing has fallen away but the tip of the nose, which Otto restores in gold. He clothes the dead emperor in white, cuts the nails, takes one tooth for a relic, and seals the tomb.
stops.quote: He was not lying, as the bodies of other dead men lie, but sat upon a throne as though living, crowned with a golden crown, holding a sceptre in gloved hands, through which his fingernails had grown and pierced.
stops.quote_source: Chronicon Novaliciense III.32 (the account of Count Otto of Lomello)
suggested_refs: Otto III enthroned (Gospels of Otto III)
the golden nose-tip of the year 1000

segments.name: The Fall of Rome, Paterno, and the Long Way Home

stops.name: Rome: the revolt, the tower speech, and exile
stops.campa: The peace does not survive the year. When Otto pardons the rebellious town of Tivoli instead of levelling it as the Romans demand, the city turns on its own emperor in February, storms his palace, and traps him inside for three days. From a tower he makes the speech Rome will remember longest: he calls them still his Romans, says he abandoned Saxony and all his own blood for their sake, led them to a greatness their fathers never reached. It does not move them. He slips out by night and rides for Ravenna, exiled from the very city he built to be eternal.
stops.quote: Are you not my Romans? For your sake I left my homeland and my kinsmen; for the love of you I have rejected my Saxons and all Germans, my own blood.
stops.quote_source: Thangmar, Vita Bernwardi c. 25 (the address from the tower, Rome 1001)
suggested_refs: The Palatine and Aventine palace ruins, site of the three-day siege
sources: History of the Germans Podcast, Episode 14

stops.name: Paterno: the fever and the death of the emperor
stops.campa: Otto spends the rest of the year gathering an army to retake Rome by force, but at Paterno, a hill-fort north of the city near Civita Castellana, a fever, malaria, most likely, the old curse of Roman campaigns, takes hold in January and will not let go. Around his bed stand Pope Sylvester, his chancellor Heribert of Cologne, and his cousin Duke Henry of Bavaria. He dies on the twenty-third or twenty-fourth of January, twenty-one years old, unmarried, without an heir of his body: the Ottonian line's whole hope narrowed in an instant to a cousin's ambition and a boy's empty throne.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Castel Paterno above the Treja valley, Faleria

stops.name: The road north to Verona: the winter cortège
stops.campa: His household will not leave him among the Romans who hated him living. They arm the body's escort as though for battle, ride out of Paterno by night, and fight their way north through a countryside that curses the corpse as it passes: stones thrown, ambushes attempted, the dead emperor's cortège shadowed the whole road by men hoping to seize the imperial insignia carried with it. They reach the safety of Verona on the seventh of February, past the worst of hostile Italy at last, while behind them in Pavia the Lombard nobles are already crowning a rival, Arduin of Ivrea, before Otto is even buried.
suggested_refs: The Lombard crown seized by Arduin of Ivrea at Pavia, February 1002
sources: History of the Germans Podcast, Episode 14

stops.name: Aachen: burial beside Charlemagne, Easter 1002
stops.campa: The cortège crosses the Alps and the length of Germany through the late winter, gathering the mourning and the ambitious both, until on Easter Sunday it reaches Aachen, the city of the boyhood coronation, the city of the opened tomb not two years past. They bury Otto before the altar of Our Lady, close by Charlemagne's own resting place, the two emperors of the Renovatio now neighbors in the same choir. He came to the throne asleep in someone's arms and leaves it the same way. Within months the German crown will pass, after a hard election, to his cousin Henry.
suggested_refs: The grave of Otto III in the choir of Aachen Cathedral
